At the surface of the conductor the potential is that of the

Hence, expanding the powers of $r$ in terms of $a$ and $F$, and

We shall begin by supposing that the conductor has a charge
 $A_{0}$, and that no external electrical force acts on it. The potential
 outside the conductor must therefore be of the form

$$\begin{equation*}
V=A_{0} \frac{1}{r}+A_{1} Y_{1}^{\prime} \frac{1}{r^{2}}+\text { \&c. }+A_{n} Y_{n}^{\prime} \frac{1}{r^{\bar{n}+1}}+\ldots, \tag{3}
\end{equation*}$$

where the surface harmonics are not assumed to be of the same
 types as in the expansion of $F$.


At the surface of the conductor the potential is that of the
 conductor, namely, the constant quantity $a$.


Hence, expanding the powers of $r$ in terms of $a$ and $F$, and
 neglecting the square and higher powers of $F$, we have

$$\begin{align*}
\alpha=A_{0} \frac{1}{a}(1-F)+A_{1} \frac{1}{u^{2}} Y_{1}^{\prime} & (1-2 F)+\text { \&c. } \\
& +A_{n} \frac{1}{u^{n+1}} Y_{n}^{\prime}(1-(n+1) F)+\ldots \tag{4}
\end{align*}$$


Since the coefficients $A_{1}$, \&c. are evidently small compared
 with $A_{0}$, we may begin by neglecting products of these co
efficients into $F$.


If we then write for $F$ in its first term its expansion in
 spherical harmonics, and equate to zero the terms involving
 harmonics of the same order, we find

$$\begin{align*}
a & =A_{0} \frac{1}{a},  \tag{5}\\
A_{1} Y_{1}^{\prime} & =A_{0} a f_{1} Y_{1}=0,  \tag{6}\\
\dot{A_{n} Y_{n}^{\prime}} & =A_{0} a^{n} f_{n} Y_{n} . \tag{7}
\end{align*}$$


It follows from these equations that the $Y^{\prime}$ 's must be of the
 same type as the $Y$ 's, and therefore identical with them, and
 that $A_{1}=0$ and $A_{n}=A_{0} \alpha^{n} f_{n}$.


To determine the density at any point of the surface, we have
 the equation

$$\begin{equation*}
4 \pi \sigma=-\frac{d V}{d \nu}=-\frac{d V}{d r} \cos \epsilon, \text { approximately } ; \tag{8}
\end{equation*}$$

where $\nu$ is the normal and $\epsilon$ is the angle which the normal makes
 with the radius. Since in this investigation we suppose $F$ and
 its first differential coefficients with respect to $\theta$ and $\phi$ to be
 small, we may put $\cos \epsilon=1$, so that

$$\begin{equation*}
4 \pi \sigma=-\frac{d V}{d r}=A_{0} \frac{1}{r^{2}}+\text { \&c. }+(n+1) A_{n} Y_{n} \frac{1}{r^{n+2}}+\ldots \tag{9}
\end{equation*}$$
